job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up for the dawn prayer, then breakfast with my flatmate Emre, and I'm at an auto parts supplier near Stuttgart by half past eight. I'm a junior embedded software engineer, so I write the small programs that run inside brake sensors. I test them on a bench with real sensors, and I have an AI assistant open the whole time to draft code and explain old code nobody documented. In the evening I work on a side project with my brother Yusuf, and on Fridays I go to the mosque and then to my parents' for dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get to this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did computer engineering at the technical university in Stuttgart, finished with a good result, and my thesis was a small controller for a model solar tracker. I did a three-month internship at the supplier, and they offered me a place in the spring. My father runs a small tile shop, my mother keeps the books, and my brother Yusuf studies business. I owe about eight thousand and I have around ten weeks of costs saved. My parents would help me if I had to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what a sensible person expects. I use AI every day, and it's good at drafts and bad at knowing what a real brake sensor does at minus twenty. At work I'd say keep using it and keep checking everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. Embedded work has a physical side, with real hardware, real tests and real safety rules, so it's hard to swap out. I'd keep growing, and my pay would creep up. The only thing I'd think about is whether the car industry here shrinks, because that's a worry whether AI exists or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and take the safety certification the company offers, because functional safety is what makes engineers hard to replace. I'd save about four hundred euros a month. And I'd keep working on the side project with Yusuf, a small tool to help tile shops quote jobs, because my father has asked for something like it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Steady. I like the life I have, and I'd be happy to just keep building it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worry about the car industry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone here knows someone in the supplier chain who got let go when electric cars changed the parts. If the company lost a big client, new people would be at risk. It's no secret, and I think about it more than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the tile shop tool.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father quotes jobs on paper, and he gets the sums wrong when he's tired. The tool takes room sizes and prices tiles in a minute. We'd charge other small shops about thirty euros a month. It's small, but it's real, and my father is proud that I'm doing it.

Keep using it and **keep checking** everything.
think: Embedded work has a **physical side**, with real hardware, tests and safety rules.
My worry is whether the **car industry** here shrinks, AI or not.
do: Save about **four hundred euros** a month.
Build the **tile shop quoting tool** with my brother.
feel: **Good and steady**, happy to keep building the life I have.

steps.text: Take the functional safety certification the company offers
Save 400 euros a month
Build the tile shop quoting tool with Yusuf
Keep writing and testing brake sensor software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, because it's going to reward people who use it well. At work I'd say we should write rules for how AI-written code gets checked. At the mosque I'd say work is a duty and learning is too, and this is the next thing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a decent position. I already work with these tools daily. A lot of the drafting I do will go to AI, and the firm might need fewer juniors. But safety-critical code needs people to test and sign it, and I can learn to be the person who does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be the team's go-to person for AI-assisted coding and write a short guide for the others. I'd move toward hardware-in-the-loop testing, which is the bench work with real parts. I'd also make the tile tool into a proper product and sign up twenty shops by next autumn. And I'd keep two months of savings in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, mostly. A bit stretched, because there's more to learn than time. But I'd take that over standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guide say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rules like: write the test first, never merge code you can't explain, and always run it on the bench. The tools are fast and sometimes confidently wrong. A guide like that helps the juniors and makes me visible to the managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our senior engineer, Herr Kessler, who's fifty-eight and doesn't use AI at all. He knows more about brake physics than anyone. I'd offer to pair with him, because I'd learn from him and he'd learn from me. We'd both be safer.

Sign up twenty shops to the **tile tool** by autumn.

steps.text: Write a one-page guide for checking AI-written code

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing in our lifetime, and I wouldn't pretend to be calm. At work I'd say we need a plan for juniors and for the whole supplier chain. At the mosque I'd ask for patience and for people to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Writing code is the first thing AI takes. In two years I think the firm could produce the same software with a tenth of the people, and I'd be in the part that's cut. The bench and the sensors would last a few years, until about 2031, but then robots arrive too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd put the tile tool in front of every small shop I can find and try to build a real income from it. I'd cut my spending hard and save every spare euro. I'd ask my father if I could work in the shop for a while, because tiling is hands-on and he knows I can lift. And I'd talk to Yusuf about turning our side project into a real company, so we have something of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stirred up, a bit sick, a bit excited. If I lose the job, I want to be in the middle of building something, not sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you build a company rather than look for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because other jobs would be shrinking too, and a company is something I can control. If the tool works, it might pay for me and Yusuf. And if it doesn't, I'd have learned how to sell, and that's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your father about working in the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Baba, I might need to work with you for a while. He'd go quiet, and then he'd say, the tiles are heavy, and I'd say, I know. We wouldn't say more. He'd just have an apron ready for me the next morning.

We need a plan for **juniors** and the supplier chain.
think: Writing code goes first, and the firm could produce the same software with **a tenth** of the people.

do: Put the **tile tool** in front of every small shop I can find.

feel: **Stirred up**, a bit sick and a bit excited.

steps.text: Pitch the quoting tool to every small tile shop in the region
Cut spending to rent, food and the train pass
Work Saturdays and weekdays in my father's tile shop if laid off
Turn all spare euros into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something real, and short enough to take seriously. At work I'd say we should hire and train juniors for the new world. At the mosque I'd say the community should help young people start businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel optimistic. In five years I could grow the tile tool into a real business with a few employees, and I'd have saved a decent cushion. I'd still be worried that big companies copy small ideas, but I'd rather compete than watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at the supplier for two years and learn as much as I can, then go half-time and run the company with Yusuf. I'd save for a deposit on a small flat, and perhaps marry in three or four years. I'd keep using AI for everything, because it's like having five more developers. And I'd put some of my savings into an index fund, so I'd own a slice of what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. I'd be a bit afraid, but I like that kind of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Yusuf bring that you don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's the business mind. He studies business and can talk to a shop owner without making them feel stupid. I'm the one who builds it. My father says we're a good pair, and I think he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why own shares, if you plan to run a company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because one company can fail. If AI makes big companies richer, I'd want some of that. Shares spread the risk, the same logic as my father buying tiles from three suppliers, not one.

The community should help young people **start businesses**.

steps.text: Stay full-time at the supplier for two more years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and I'd say let's build things. At work I'd say let's plan a career ladder for juniors that includes AI skills. At the mosque I'd say each of us should learn something new each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel excellent. I'd be 32, and with ten years I'd have a company, a family and maybe a second language. I'd worry only about complacency, and about my parents getting older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the supplier for three or four years, then move to the company full-time. I'd buy a flat, marry, and help my parents retire from the shop. I'd also invest each month and take courses in management, since I'd have staff someday. And I'd keep a close eye on the date, because ten years can drift into nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled and happy. I'd feel like the road was long enough to walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you help your parents retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father is sixty and would like to stop in about eight years. We'd either hire a manager for the shop or sell it, and I'd cover the gap if the money is short. In my family, children look after parents, and I want to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the long timeline a trap in any way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It could make me soft. I'd keep a rule: every year at Ramadan I look at what I've built and what I've learned, and I fix the gap before the next year.

Each of us should **learn something new** every year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to build up enough income from my own work and I'd be asking my family for help. What would help is customers for small firms like our tool, easy business rules, a community that backs new businesses, and a company that tells juniors early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think someone who uses AI all day must be a believer. I'm not a believer. I'm a worker who found a good tool, and I'd like to be the one who owns something when it changes the world.

headlineQuote: I'm not a believer. I'm a worker who found a good tool, and I'd like to be the one who owns something when it changes the world.
portrait: Umar Weber is **22**, a junior embedded engineer at an auto parts supplier near Stuttgart, sharing a flat.
He did computer engineering, owes about **eight thousand** and has ten weeks of costs saved.
He's traditional and adaptive: faith, family and work are central, and he uses **AI every day**.
He builds a side tool for his father's **tile shop** with his brother, and it's his plan in nearly every scenario.
His mood is calm in most worlds and **anxious** at AGI in two years, when he'd join his father's shop.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have **no time** to build his own income.
whatWouldHelp: **Customers** for small firms, easy business rules, community backing and early honesty from his company.
